subject: Anatomy
summary: The thoracic duct is the main conduit for lymph and dietary fat from the abdomen to the venous system. It runs from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen to the left venous angle, where it empties into the bloodstream.

sections.p: The thoracic duct transports chyle—lymph rich in triglycerides—plus immune cells from the lower body and left side of the thorax to the systemic circulation.
b: ≈ 38‑45 cm long, the longest lymphatic vessel
Carries ~2 L of lymph per day in adults

sections.p: It begins as the cisterna chyli at L2, ascends through the aortic hiatus, runs right of the vertebral bodies, crosses to the left at T5‑T6, and ends at the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).
b: Crosses behind the aortic arch and esophagus
Enters the neck at the left scalene tubercle

sections.p: In the superior mediastinum it lies posterior to the left brachiocephalic vein and anterior to the vertebral column, adjacent to the azygos system, vagus and phrenic nerves, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
b: Close to the left brachiocephalic vein

sections.p: Small arterial branches arise from the thoracic aorta and intercostal arteries, supplying the duct wall.
b: Branches from the aorta at T4‑T6

sections.p: Autonomic fibers from the sympathetic trunk modulate lymphatic contractility; somatic afferents travel with the vagus nerve.
Collects lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left head/neck, and all intestinal chyle, delivering it to the venous system for immune surveillance and nutrient distribution.
Disruption or obstruction produces chylothorax, lymphatic leak, or lymphedema. Recognising milky pleural fluid with triglycerides >110 mg/dL is key.

t.b: Is the effusion chylous? Triglycerides >110 mg/dL confirm chylothorax; if unavailable, milky appearance plus high lymphocyte count suggests it.
Where is the leak? Shows duct disruption; if imaging not available, use CT thorax to look for mediastinal fluid collections.
Is there a pleural effusion? Detects fluid; a left‑sided opacification raises suspicion for chylothorax.

sections.p: Know the course, termination, and typical causes of chylothorax. Be able to differentiate chylous from empyema and transudative effusions.
b: Milky pleural fluid + TG >110 mg/dL = chylothorax

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden massive left‑sided pleural effusion causing respiratory distress
Unexplained high‑output lymph leak after thoracic surgery
Signs of severe malnutrition from chronic chyle loss

faq.q: Why does chylothorax usually appear on the left side?
faq.a: The thoracic duct empties into the left venous angle; injury near its termination releases chyle into the left pleural space.

faq.q: Can a thoracic duct injury be managed without surgery?
faq.a: Yes, conservative measures (dietary fat restriction, medium‑chain triglycerides, pleural drainage) succeed in many cases; surgery is reserved for persistent leaks.

faq.q: What distinguishes chylous from empyema fluid?
faq.a: Chylous fluid is milky with high triglycerides; empyema is purulent, high neutrophils, and low triglycerides.

exam: Describe the anatomical course of the thoracic duct and its termination point.
Explain how you would confirm a suspected chylothorax and the next management steps.
List three common causes of thoracic duct injury and one preventive measure for each.
